INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
Everytown for Gun Safety (formally, Everytown
for Gun Safety Action Fund) is the nation’s largest
gun-violence-prevention organization, with more than
eleven million supporters across the country. Everytown was founded in 2014 as the combined effort of
Mayors Against Illegal Guns, a national, bipartisan
coalition of mayors combating illegal guns and gun
trafficking, and Moms Demand Action for Gun Sense
in America, an organization formed after a gunman
used an assault weapon to murder twenty children
and six adults at Sandy Hook Elementary School in
Newtown, Connecticut. Everytown also includes a
large network of gun-violence survivors who are empowered to share their stories and advocate for responsible gun laws, as well as a national movement of
high school and college students working to end gun
violence.
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF
ARGUMENT
Assault weapons are a highly destructive means
of mass violence in modern America: all ten of the
highest-casualty mass shootings in the United States
in the last decade have involved an assault weapon.
These military-style weapons are designed for the battlefield to inflict maximum damage on the human
body in the shortest amount of time.

1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in
part, and no entity or person, other than amicus curiae, its members, and its counsel, made a monetary contribution intended to
fund the preparation or submission of this brief.

2

Our Constitution and history reflect the obvious
wisdom that democratically elected government bodies can keep these weapons of war out of our communities. In turn, for the reasons set out in respondents’
briefs, prohibiting assault weapons is constitutional
under the Second Amendment analysis established in
New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, 597 U.S.
1 (2022). See Conn. Resp. Br. 9-37; Cook Cnty. Resp.
Br. 13-46. Everytown submits this amicus brief to address two issues.
First, this brief expands on one strand of historical
evidence supporting the principles that underlie the
challenged laws: restrictions on armed groups. Although our nation has endured mass violence throughout its history, that violence has assumed different
shapes across generations as technologies developed
and social concerns evolved. Today, mass violence can
be perpetrated in minutes—or even seconds—by a single individual with an assault weapon. Before the
20th century, however, mass violence was primarily
carried out by groups of individuals armed with far
more rudimentary weapons, such as bludgeons,
blades, and guns that fired just one or a small number
of rounds. Restrictions on armed groups, operating
primarily through the common law crimes of riot and
unlawful assembly, thus responded to the dangers of
mass violence that faced Americans in the 18th and
19th centuries. As more specific threats of armedgroup violence emerged, such as threats posed by private militias and the Ku Klux Klan, American legislatures responded with statutes to address those
threats.
Together, these restrictions demonstrate that
laws restricting the means of perpetrating mass

3

murder and terror have always been part of our nation’s historical tradition. Equally, this history explains why regulatory responses did not always focus
on specific weapons: when the weapons were rudimentary, targeting group conduct was a tailored and effective response. And our nation’s historical tradition
also includes a long tradition of restricting especially
dangerous weapons. See Conn. Resp. Br. 10-23; Cook
Cnty. Resp. Br. 15-25. Both historical strands reflect
and embody the principle that governments have the
authority—consistent with the Second Amendment—
to protect the public from the means of mass violence.
Second, post-ratification evidence is a crucial part
of the Second Amendment historical analysis, regardless of whether the founding or Reconstruction era is
the central focus of that analysis. The Court should
consider that evidence here. Moreover, as with prior
decisions, the Court need not decide which period to
prioritize in the event of an irreconcilable conflict because the historical record is consistent across time. If
it were to decide the issue, however, the Court should
conclude that the Reconstruction era has primacy,
consistent with originalist principles.
ARGUMENT
I. HISTORICAL RESTRICTIONS ON ARMED GROUPS
ARE ANALOGOUS TO MODERN ASSAULT WEAPON
PROHIBITIONS
As respondents have explained, the challenged assault weapon prohibitions are “consistent with the
principles that underpin our regulatory tradition.”
United States v. Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680, 692 (2024); see
Conn. Resp. Br. 9-37; Cook Cnty. Resp. Br. 13-46.
These principles are embodied in multiple regulatory

4

traditions, including restrictions on weapon types and
prohibitions on armed groups. “Taken together,”
Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 698, these traditions confirm that
the challenged assault weapon laws are consistent
with our constitutional principles.
A. Before the 20th Century, Mass Violence
Was Perpetrated by Armed Groups
 For much of our nation’s history—from the founding era, through Reconstruction, and into the 20th
century—mass violence was “a group activity.” Barnett v. Raoul, 180 F.4th 1035, 1057 (7th Cir. 2026) (citation omitted); see Grant Pet. App. 43a; Grant C.A.
App. 1165-66 ¶41 (Roth Decl.). Because the weapons
that existed in early America “were ‘certainly lethal
but did not provide individuals … the means to inflict
mass casualties on their own,’” people gathered together in groups to accomplish their violent ends.
Bianchi v. Brown, 111 F.4th 438, 463 (4th Cir. 2024)
(en banc), cert. denied, 145 S. Ct. 1534 (2025) (citation
omitted); see Grant Pet. App. 43a; Grant C.A. App.
1165-66 ¶41. Today, “a single person armed with an
AR-15 can … unleash the same lethal potential as dozens if not hundreds of eighteenth-century assailants,”
and “carry[] out a mass murder in seconds.” Darrell A.
H. Miller et al., Lethality and the Historical Principles
of Arms Regulation, 54 Pepp. L. Rev. (forthcoming),
https://tinyurl.com/efrts97 (manuscript at 34) (emphasis omitted); Grant Pet. App. 43a. But historically
it was these armed groups that were “[t]he only way
to kill a large number of people.” Grant C.A. App.
1165-66 ¶41.
America’s history of mass violence traces back to
England, which experienced riots for centuries. Paul
A. Gilje, Rioting in America 13-15 (1996). In the 18th

5

century, for example, groups in England rioted about
political, economic, and labor issues. Id. at 15-16.
Some of the deadliest riots concerned religion, such as
the 1780 anti-Catholic Gordon Riots, in which mobs of
demonstrators, many of them armed, caused widespread destruction in London; close to 300 people died.
George F.E. Rudé, The Gordon Riots: A Study of the
Rioters and their Victims, 6 Transactions of the Royal
Hist. Soc’y 93, 97-99, 103 (1956).
Similar unrest traveled across the ocean to America, where the colonies also experienced group violence. During the 17th century, for example, an armed
group of Marylanders sacked and burned Lewes, Delaware in a land dispute, and a group of women in Marblehead, Massachusetts bludgeoned two Native
American men to death. See Gilje, supra, at 19-20. Rioting was especially prevalent in the leadup to the
American Revolution, with at least 150 riots occurring
between 1765 and 1769, some leaving cities nearly ungovernable for weeks at a time. See id. at 35, 38-41.
Into the 1770s, riots were used in revolutionary efforts
against the British (supported, at least to a degree, by
American elites). See id. at 45-49.
After the Revolution, a depressed economy and
high taxes to pay war debts led to a wave of defaults
and foreclosures. Armed groups in Massachusetts responded by blocking court sessions and foreclosure
sales. Alan Taylor, American Revolutions: A Continental History, 1750-1804 367 (2016). The difficulties
Massachusetts had dealing with the largest of these
uprisings, Shays’s Rebellion, led many—including
elites who had supported revolutionary riots—to understand the need for a stronger central government
and support a constitutional convention. See Jill

6

Lepore, These Truths: A History of the United States
117-18 (2018); Gilje, supra, at 54. And soon after the
ratification of the Constitution, the federal government used its newfound powers to suppress the Whiskey Rebellion, an armed tax revolt in Pennsylvania.
See Saul Cornell, A Well-Regulated Militia: The
Founding Fathers and the Origins of Gun Control in
America 76-85 (2006); Gilje, supra, at 55. By this
point, most major leaders agreed that mobs should not
“dictat[e] the course of government through extra-legal violence.” See Gilje, supra, at 54.
Mob violence nevertheless continued during the
antebellum period. It was often directed at protecting
the institution of slavery and the subjugation of Black
Americans, targeting both abolitionists and free
Blacks in the North. See, e.g., Kate Masur, Until Justice Be Done: America’s First Civil Rights Movement,
From the Revolution to Reconstruction 99-100 (2021).
As one example, in 1834, mobs in New York armed
“with brickbats and other missiles” attacked abolitionists and the Black community—severely damaging or destroying sixty buildings, including six
churches. Linda K. Kerber, Abolitionists & Amalgamators: The New York City Race Riots of 1834, 48
N.Y. Hist. 28, 30-33 (1967); Daniel Walker Howe,
What Hath God Wrought: The Transformation of
America, 1815-1848 433 (2007). Mob violence was also
prevalent in the South, and typically more deadly. See
Howe, supra, at 435.
These horrific incidents did not go unnoticed. In
an 1838 speech, a 28-year-old Abraham Lincoln observed that “[a]ccounts of outrages committed by
mobs form the everyday news of the times,” and
warned that “[w]henever the vicious portion of the

7

population shall be permitted” to gather and commit
acts of terror and violence, such as to “shoot editors,
and hang and burn obnoxious persons at pleasure and
with impunity, depend on it, this government cannot
last.” Id. at 438.
Mass killings by armed groups became more prevalent during this period as well. See Grant C.A. App.
1165-67 ¶¶41-42. In 1844, for example, an attack on
Philadelphia’s Catholic community left twenty dead
and destroyed Catholic homes and churches throughout the city. Randolph Roth, American Homicide 188,
305 (2009). And in 1855, a riot initiated by nativist
Protestants against Irish and German Catholics in
Louisville, Kentucky, resulted in twenty-two deaths.
David Grimsted, American Mobbing, 1828-1861: Toward Civil War 232-34 (1998).
In the years after the Civil War, armed mob violence often took the form of mass killings of freedmen
and others in the South by white supremacist groups.
Grant C.A. App. 1167-68 ¶43. In one incident in New
Orleans, armed white mobs fired on a group of delegates and supporters, most of them Black, assembling
for Louisiana’s constitutional convention and then
stormed the convention, indiscriminately shooting attendees and killing thirty-seven people. Eric Foner,
Reconstruction: America’s Unfinished Revolution 262-
63 (1988). In Opelousas, Louisiana, attacks by armed
white paramilitary groups seeking to destroy the local
Republican party left an estimated 250 people dead.
Lorraine Boissoneault, The Deadliest Massacre in Reconstruction-Era Louisiana Happened 150 Years Ago,
Smithsonian Mag. (Sept. 28, 2018). Sometimes the violence from armed groups was smaller in scale but
equally terrifying, as groups like the Ku Klux Klan

8

engaged in assassinations and murders throughout
the South. Foner, supra, at 342.
Mass killings by armed groups also plagued other
parts of the nation in the postbellum period and beyond. Out west, for example, Chinese workers were
frequently attacked, such as in 1885 when an armed
white mob in Rock Springs, Wyoming killed twentyeight Chinese workers, wounded fifteen more, and
looted and burned all of the homes in Rock Springs’s
Chinatown. Tom Rea, The Rock Springs Massacre,
WyoHistory.org (Nov. 8, 2014) , perma.cc/ST2A-
PBNH. Mass killings remained a threat into the early
20th century—with the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre, in
which an armed white mob murdered more than 300
Black Americans, the most notable example.  See
Grant C.A. App. 1168 ¶43.
All told, our communities have long endured the
horrors of mass violence. But today, a single gunman
armed with an assault weapon can murder dozens in
minutes. “Early firearms by themselves,” by contrast,
“did not facilitate mass killings.” Grant Pet. App. 43a.
Thus, “[u]ntil very recently, there was no real ability
to perpetrate mass violence with weapons except
through the coordinated violent behavior of groups.”
Miller, supra, at 38. And historically, governments responded to these threats through common law and
legislative restrictions on armed groups—as the following section explains.

9

B. Throughout Anglo-American History,
Courts and Legislatures Addressed Group
Mass Violence by Restricting Armed
Groups
In England, and later in the United States, governments recognized the serious public safety threat
posed by armed groups. Accordingly, like the modern
jurisdictions that prohibit assault weapons, they limited the means of committing acts of mass violence
through common law and legislative restrictions on
armed groups—even if those groups had not engaged
in actual violence. These restrictions preceded the
first American colonies, were widely adopted in America during the colonial period and founding era,
evolved to address the mass violence dangers of the
Civil War and Reconstruction periods, remained in effect into the 20th century, and continue to exist in
some form today. These laws are antecedents of modern assault weapon prohibitions, which target the
modern mass violence phenomena of mass shootings.
1. Armed groups were prosecuted as riots
or unlawful assemblies under English
common law
Under English common law, public gatherings
were generally lawful. Certain conduct, however,
could convert a legal gathering into an illegal one—
including the fact that the group was armed. Other
conduct of the group determined the precise category
of illegality—whether it was as a “riot,” a “rout,” or an
“unlawful assembly”—but as to each category, the fact
that participants were armed could render an otherwise lawful gathering illegal.

10

William Hawkins, in his “widely read 1716 treatise,” Bruen, 597 U.S. at 45, explained that a riot was
“a tumultuous disturbance of the peace, by three persons, or more, assembling … with an intent mutually
to assist one another” in a goal of a “private nature,
and afterwards actually executing the same in a violent and turbulent manner, to the terror of the people,” regardless of whether the goal was “of itself lawful or unlawful.” 1 William Hawkins, A Treatise of the
Pleas of the Crown 155 (1716) (capitalizations altered
in all Hawkins quotations). Crucially, the group’s being armed was one of the ways to show a violent and
turbulent manner. As Hawkins explained:
[I]t seems to be clearly agreed, that in every
riot there must be some such circumstances,
either of actual force or violence, or at least of
an apparent tendency thereto, as are naturally apt to strike a terror into the people, as
the shew of armour, threatening speeches or
turbulent gestures; for every such offense
must be laid to be done in terrorem populi[.]
Id. at 157 (emphasis added).2
The term “armour,” historically, included weapons as well as defensive coverings. See “Armour,” Oxford English Dictionary, oed.com (“I.1 The whole

2 Other English treatises and legal dictionaries set out similar principles. One 16th-century writer, for example, explained
that riots, routs, and unlawful assemblies all required a gathering of three or more people and that “their being together doe
breed some apparant disturbance of the Peace,” such as by “shew
of Armour, … so that either the peaceable sort of men bee unquieted and feared by the fact” or the less peaceable be “emboldened
by the example.” William Lambard, Eirenarcha: Or of the Office
of the Justices of Peace 186-87 (1591).

11

apparatus of war collectively; military equipment,
both offensive and defensive; arms, weaponry.”).3 And
context indicates that simply being armed was sufficient for a “shew of armour.”4 Accordingly, a group’s
being armed could itself establish that the circumstances had an apparent tendency to violence, and
thus were naturally apt to cause terror. (That is certainly the understanding that took root in this country. In the equivalent passage of his influential 19thcentury treatise, Francis Wharton wrote:
It must be shown that the assembling as accompanied with some such circumstances, either of actual force or violence, or at least of
an apparent tendency thereto, as were calculated to inspire people with terror, such as being armed, using threatening speeches, turbulent gestures, or the like.
Francis Wharton, A Treatise on the Criminal Law of
the United States 524 (1846) (emphasis added).)5

3 See also id. (including as examples “Their armour for war
is a bow and arrows” (1761) and “Spear, or halberd, seems to
have been anciently a common piece of warlike armour” (1769)).
4 The inclusion of “turbulent gestures” separately from “armour” indicates that the simple wearing of arms, without gesturing with those arms—i.e., without brandishing them—brought
an armed group within the prohibition.
5 An early-19th-century English treatise likewise recognized that Hawkins’s reference to “shew of armour” meant “being
armed.” John Frederick Archbold, A Summary of the Law Relative to Pleading and Evidence in Criminal Cases 333 (1822) (stating that a group “being armed” had a “tendency … to inspire people with terror” (citing Hawkins)).

12

In short, being armed as a group inspired terror
in a way that, Bruen concluded, being armed as an individual did not. Bruen interpreted English sources,
including Hawkins, to indicate that the in terrorem
populi element “require[d] something more than
merely carrying a firearm in public” for an individual.
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 50 (discussing Sir John Knight’s
Case); id. at 45 (“Hawkins … confirmed that ‘no wearing of Arms is within the meaning of [the Statute of
Northampton], unless it be accompanied with such
Circumstances as are apt to terrify the People.’” (alteration in original) (quoting Hawkins, supra, at
136)). And Bruen saw “no reason to think that the
founding generation held a different view.” Id. at 50.
But Hawkins, and the American sources that adopted
his views, compel the conclusion that being armed
could supply the terror element when a group, and not
just an individual, was armed.
Hawkins further confirmed that an armed group
was naturally apt to create public terror in his discussion of unlawful assemblies.6 He wrote that “any
meeting … of great numbers of people with such circumstances of terror, as cannot but endanger the public peace … seems properly to be called an unlawful
assembly,” and gave as an example the situation
“where great numbers, complaining of a common
grievance, meet together, armed in a warlike manner,
in order to consult together concerning the most
proper means for the recovery of their interests; for no
one can foresee what may be the event of such an

6 Although a “riot” generally required a group to share a
common goal and act to accomplish that goal, an armed group
could still be an “unlawful assembly” even without joint action.
Compare Hawkins, supra, at 155, with id. at 158.

13

assembly.” Hawkins, supra, at 158 (emphasis added).
Other treatises repeated this example. See, e.g., 19
Charles Viner, A General Abridgement of Law and Equity 234 (2d ed. 1793); 4 Thomas Walter Williams, The
Whole Law Relative to the Duty and Office of a Justice
of the Peace 30 (1795).
The specific case Hawkins was describing in this
passage was Howard v. Bell (1616) 80 Eng. Rep. 241,
242; Hob. 91, 92 (Star Chamber); see Hawkins, supra,
at 158 (citing “Hob. 92” in margin). There, the court
approved fines for “assembling the tenants to the
number of 200 in an open field … divers of the[m] …
being weaponed with swords and daggers, abiding
three hours together, and yet nothing was proved
done there by any of the defendants, but conference
concerning the defence of their title.” 80 Eng. Rep. at
242. A treatise described another case in which eighty
people gathered “with Spades, Matocks , Pistols,
Swords and Daggers” and made trenches to release
water from an illegal weir across the river Trent. See
Michael Dalton, The Country Justice 324-25 (1690).
Even though “it w[as] lawful to make the trenches,”
they were “deeply fined in the Star-Chamber” because
“they came with such number, and weapons.” Id. As
these cases illustrate, assembling with ordinary
weapons—such as swords and daggers—was sufficient to trigger the prohibition. And given that Hawkins was describing Howard, “weaponed with swords
and daggers”—ordinary weapons—is what he meant
when he described the group as “armed in a warlike
manner.” 80 Eng. Rep. at 242; Hawkins, supra, at 158.
Courts likewise stressed that the group nature of
the conduct was important to its illegality. In Regina
v. Soley, for example, Lord Chief Justice Holt

14

explained that “[i]f a number of men assemble with
arms, in terrorem populi, though no act is done, it is a
riot. If three come out of an ale-house and go armed, it
is a riot.” (1707) 88 Eng. Rep. 935, 936-37 (QB). He
recognized that the law treated a single armed individual differently than an armed group, noting that
“[t]hough a man may ride with arms, yet he cannot
take two with him to defend himself.” Id. at 937.
Soley also highlighted another important aspect of
the English common law of riot: it could prohibit an
individual from riding with an armed group “even
though his life is threatened”—i.e., there was no exception for self-defense outside the home. See id. Likewise, in Semayne’s Case, the court concluded that it
was unlawful for someone to “assemble his friends
and neighbors … to go with him to the market, or elsewhere for his safeguard against violence.” (1604) 77
Eng. Rep. 194, 195 (KB). A 17th-century treatise similarly made clear that “albeit one be threatened, and
in danger of his life, and to defend himself[] he gathers
a force, and they ride about armed; this is a Riot.” William Shepherd, The Whole Office of the Country Justice of Peace 55 (2d ed. 1652); see also Hawkins, supra,
at 158 (“[A]n assembly of a man’s friends for the defence of his person, against those who threaten to beat
him if he go to such a market, &c. is unlawful[.]”).7

7 These sources acknowledged that gathering a group for
self-defense in one’s home was legal. See Semayne’s Case, 77 Eng.
Rep. at 195; Shepherd, supra, at 55 (discussing an armed group
specifically); Hawkins, supra, at 158.

15

2. Common law and statutes in early
America punished armed groups to
prevent mass violence
Concern about mass violence and restrictions on
armed groups crossed the Atlantic with the colonists.
See Miller, supra, at 33 (describing historical prohibitions on unlawful assemblies, riots, and “companies of
armed individuals”). Treatises made clear that three
or more individuals assembling together for a common
goal (including a lawful goal) would be a riot if there
were “circumstances of actual force or violence, or at
least of an apparent tendency thereto, as are naturally apt to strike a terror into the people; [such] as
the shew of armour.” 1 William Oldnall Russell & Daniel Davis, A Treatise on Crimes & Misdemeanors 351-
52 (1824) (emphasis added). In other words, the fact
that the group was armed contributed the “apparent
tendency” to violence sufficient for their actions to be
“in terrorem populi.” Id. at 352; see also J.A.G. Davis,
A Treatise on Criminal Law 252 (1838).
As in England, even if not all the elements of a riot
were met, armed gatherings could be illegal as an “unlawful assembly.” See J.A.G. Davis, supra, at 254-55
(reiterating Hawkins’s example of a group “armed in
a warlike manner” constituting an unlawful assembly). And regardless of the categorization, “being
armed” was one of the “circumstances” that could evidence “an apparent tendency [to violence] … as were
calculated to inspire people with terror,” and transform an otherwise lawful assembly into an illegal one.
See Wharton, supra, at 524; see also, e.g., State v. Alexander, 41 S.C.L. (7 Rich.) 5, 8 (S.C. App. L. 1853)
(noting, in a riot case, that “[a] show of arms … [is]
one of the circumstances which are calculated to

16

produce alarm”); Commonwealth v. Runnels, 10 Mass.
518, 520 (1813) (“[I]n indictments for that species of
riots which consist in going about armed, &c., without
committing any act, the words [in terrorem populi] …
are necessary, because the offence consists in terrifying the public[.]”).
American colonies and early states codified somewhat narrower restrictions in statutes but continued
to prosecute the common law offenses. In 1750, a colonial Massachusetts statute provided that if “[t]welve
or more [people], being Arm’d with Clubs or other
Weapons, or if … Fifty or upwards [people], whether
armed or not, shall be unlawfully[,] riotously or tumultuously assembled,” and an official read an order
to disperse, then any who did not disperse could be
arrested and punished (and if officials killed or injured anyone resisting, the officials would be “indemnified and held guiltless”). 1749-51 Mass. Acts 339. In
doing so, Massachusetts recognized the special dangers posed by armed groups, even those with rudimentary weapons, compared to unarmed groups. After independence, Massachusetts adopted a similar law.
See 1786 Mass. Acts 502. Several other states followed
suit. See, e.g., 1791 N.H. Laws 277, 280-81 (restriction
applying to armed groups of twelve or more and unarmed groups of thirty or more) (passed Feb. 16,
1791); 1797 N.J. Laws 179-80; 1838-39 Wis. Sess.
Laws 368-69; Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 12, ch. 159, § 5 (1840);
Mich. Rev. Stat. tit. 30, ch. 157, § 1 (1846); R.I. Rev.
Stat. tit. 30, ch. 213 § 1 (1857); 1 David Wagner, The
Statutes of the State of Missouri, art. 7, ch. 42, § 10–
11 (1870).
These statutes did not replace the common law
crime; instead, they were “another and distinct

17

Russell, 45 N.H. 83, 85 (1863). In Russell, the defendants challenged the indictment as failing to allege
that “a proclamation under the riot act had been
made.” Id. The court explained that no such proclamation was necessary for a prosecution under the common law. Id. The statutory offense was a “new and
distinct offence” with a harsher punishment: in New
Hampshire, “both fine and imprisonment” (and in
England, death). Id. But common law riot, a misdemeanor with no proclamation-and-failure-to-disperse
requirement, remained an offense. Id.; see also id. at
85-86 (finding no indication of intent to repeal the
common law, including by reference to 1791 and 1829

(Old Bailey) (explaining that “a riot is not the less a
riot … because the proclamation of the Riot Act has
not been read,” but is, in that circumstance, a misdemeanor rather than a capital offense); Wharton, supra, at 525 (citing Fursey’s explanation in U.S. treatise).
American courts enforced both statutory and common law restrictions to punish those who took part in
armed groups. In one case, for example, a group of
men assembled outside a house “in search of somebody they thought [was] there,” and “[a]ll were
armed.” Sanders v. State, 60 Ga. 126, 128 (1878). “The
man of the house was frightened, and tried to pacify
them, and hence invited them in and gave them
breakfast.” Id. The Supreme Court of Georgia concluded that the evidence was “enough … to make riot

18

under our Code,” albeit as a close case, and affirmed
the judgment of conviction. Id.8
In another case, a dispute between an individual,
Marsh, who had erected a dam partially on the land
of another named Brooks, led to a prosecution for riot.
See State v. Brooks, 19 S.C.L. (1 Hill) 361, 362 (S.C.
App. L. & Eq. 1833). Brooks “armed himself and the
other defendants,” went to the location of the dam,
“said he intended to cut the dam—and that he would
not be insulted on his own land: and would do it, at all
hazards,” and did cut the dam. Id. After describing the
common law offense of riot as set out in Hawkins’s
treatise—including that the group’s goal could be, “of
itself, lawful”—the court concluded that these facts
“make out the offence, in the very terms of the definition.” Id.9
In these cases and others, a threat to public peace
arose from the fact that the group was armed. And as
the court stressed in United States v. Fenwick, 25 F.
Cas. 1062 (C.C.D.C. 1836) (No. 15,086), laws restricting such actions were important in preventing mass
violence, because “[w]hen a mob is once raised, no one
can tell where it will end, and all who assisted in

C. Historical Restrictions on Armed Groups
Are Part of the Robust Historic Lineage for
Modern Assault Weapon Laws
 This Court has made clear that “[t]he regulatory
challenges posed by firearms today are not always the
same as those that preoccupied the Founders in 1791
or the Reconstruction generation in 1868.” Bruen, 597
U.S. at 27. Mass violence has plagued our country
since before its founding, but has taken different
forms over time. As Judge St. Eve explained for the
Seventh Circuit in Barnett:
When the Second and Fourteenth Amendments were ratified, mass killings were a
‘group activity,’ relying on ‘primitive firearms
and melee weapons’ because individuals

Historical restrictions on armed groups thus “reveal a principle,” Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 740 (Barrett, J.,

see also Wolford v. Lopez, 609 U.S. 185, 197 (2026).
Armed groups restrictions are analogous to assault weapons prohibitions both as to their “why” and
“how.” The “why”—the “rationale” of each law, Wolford, 609 U.S. at 196—is the same for both: preventing
mass-casualty violence and terror. And the “how”—
“that is, whether [the historical law] imposed a restriction similar to that imposed by the challenged

with the means for self-defense as individuals. See
Soley, 88 Eng. Rep. at 937 (“Though a man may ride
with arms, yet he cannot take two with him to defend

24

himself.”); supra at 14 (explaining that historical laws

In short, both the historical and modern laws reflect
the same principle: throughout our nation’s history,
legislatures have protected communities from the
threat of mass violence by regulating the means of
committing that violence.
Petitioners, for their part, do not seriously dispute
that mass shootings are a recent societal problem. See
Pet. Br. 41. But they overlook that this “distinction[]”
carries “important consequences for how a legislature
might respond” to mass violence consistent with historical tradition. Barnett, 180 F.4th at 1057. “States
adopt laws to address the problems that confront
them,” McCullen v. Coakley, 573 U.S. 464, 481 (2014)
(citation omitted), and the Second Amendment is not
“a law trapped in amber,” Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 691.
Accordingly, “a State … can respond” to the problems
before it “with focused regulations to address the
threat.” Wolford, 609 U.S. at 220 (Barrett, J., concurring). That is precisely what Connecticut and Cook
County have done. Historical legislatures focused on
the mechanism that was “principally responsible” for
the mass violence before them—they “target[ed]
armed groups.” Barnett, 180 F.4th 1057. And modern
legislatures have likewise calibrated their response to
the “central cause of [the] mass carnage” before them
by prohibiting assault weapons. Bianchi, 111 F.4th at
463.
In short, the historical armed groups prohibitions
bolster and elucidate the longstanding historical pedigree for modern assault weapon laws—particularly
given the evolving threat of mass violence. These restrictions sit alongside historical prohibitions on

25

unusually dangerous weapons in confirming that assault weapons may be banned. See Conn. Resp. Br. 10-
23, 33-37; Cook Cnty. Resp. Br. 13-46; Rahimi, 602
U.S. at 698 (relying on two historical strands “[t]aken
together” in rejecting Second Amendment challenge);
see also Wolford, 609 U.S. at 196 (noting that a modern restriction may rest on an “analogue or collection
of analogues”). Because democratically enacted legislatures are entitled to apply “the balance struck by the
founding generation to modern circumstances,”
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 29 n.7, the challenged assault
weapon laws should be upheld.
II. RECONSTRUCTION-ERA AND LATER HISTORICAL
EVIDENCE IS A CRUCIAL PART OF THE BRUEN ANAL-
YSIS
This Court has made clear that post-ratification
history “is a critical tool of constitutional interpretation.” Bruen, 597 U.S. at 20 (quoting District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 605 (2008)). Yet petitioners seek to confine this Court’s historical analysis
strictly to the founding era. See Pet. Br. 40-41, 46, 49.
Doing so flies in the face of precedent and originalist
principles.
A. The Court Should Give Significant Weight
to Post-Ratification History, Regardless of
Which Era is the Focus
The “great weight” this Court affords post-ratification history in the “proper interpretation of constitutional provisions,” Chiafalo v. Washington, 591 U.S.
578, 592-93 (2020) (citation omitted), extends to the
Second Amendment. Starting with Heller, Justice
Scalia’s opinion for the Court examined caselaw, public discourse, and commentary on the Second

26

Amendment “through the end of the 19th century.”
Heller, 554 U.S. at 605, 610, 614, 616-19. Bruen then
relied on mid- to late-19th-century cases and statutes,
and “public discourse surrounding Reconstruction.”
597 U.S. at 30, 51-55, 60. The Court likewise consulted post-ratification history in its subsequent Second Amendment cases. For example, in United States
v. Hemani, 608 U.S. 772 (2026), it considered laws,
cases, treatises, and social practices from the mid- to
late-19th century. See id. at 783-84, 787 n.4, 788 n.5;
see also Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 695-96 (relying on laws
passed between 1836 and 1868, including by reference
to Bruen, 597 U.S. at 56 & n.23).
This Court’s cases thus make clear that post-ratification history is highly relevant to Second Amendment analysis. And for good reason: considering postratification history advances Bruen’s originalist inquiry in at least three ways.
First, as Heller recognized, later history offers valuable insight into the original public meaning of the
right because later generations were steeped in founding-era understandings. 554 U.S. at 614 (noting that
the understandings of those “born and educated in the
early 19th century” are “instructive”). After all,
“[p]rinciples of liberty fundamental enough to have
been embodied within constitutional guarantees are
not readily erased from the Nation’s consciousness.”
Nev. Comm’n on Ethics v. Carrigan, 564 U.S 117, 122
(2011) (citation omitted).
Second, post-ratification history can “liquidate
[and] settle the meaning of disputed or indeterminate
terms [and] phrases in the Constitution.” Bruen, 597
U.S. at 35-36 (cleaned up). Indeed, “the Framers
themselves intended that postratification history

27

would shed light on the meaning of vague constitutional text.” Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 725 (Kavanaugh, J.,
concurring).
Third, and relatedly, later history can liquidate
constitutional meaning because the absence of legislation in an earlier period does not demonstrate that
people believed such legislation would be unconstitutional. Petitioners’ contrary suggestion has the “serious problem[]” of “assum[ing] that founding-era legislatures maximally exercised their power to regulate.”
Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 739-40 (Barrett, J., concurring).
In fact, this Court has repeatedly confirmed that the
absence of legislation does not indicate that legislation was thought to be unconstitutional. See, e.g.,
Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Org., 597 U.S. 215,
253 (2022) (rejecting inference of unconstitutionality
from absence of 18th- and 19th-century abortion restrictions); Amicus Br. of U.S. Conf. of Cath. Bishops
17-18; see also Zuber v. Allen, 396 U.S. 168, 185 n.21
(1969) (“Congressional inaction frequently betokens
unawareness, preoccupation, or paralysis.”).
Nevertheless, petitioners say that even laws from
as early as 1837 are “too late” under Bruen. Pet. Br.
46. But Bruen had found substantial, affirmative evidence that people with ordinary self-defense needs
had a right to carry in public, see, e.g., 597 U.S. at 53-
57, and dismissed a few later laws because they “contradict[ed] the overwhelming weight of other evidence,” id. at 65-66. Short of that untenable use, precedent and originalist principles require giving meaningful weight to post-ratification history.

28

B. Historical Analysis Should Focus on the
Reconstruction Era
This Court has left open whether to privilege the
founding or Reconstruction era in Second Amendment
analysis. See Hemani, 608 U.S. at 783 n.3; Rahimi,
602 U.S. at 692 n.1; Bruen, 597 U.S. at 37-38; see also
Wolford, 609 U.S. at 221 n.7 (Barrett, J., concurring).
It can do the same here, because the history “runs in
an unbroken line from medieval England to the
Founding to the Reconstruction era to the twentieth
century.” Conn. Resp. Br. 6. If the Court reaches the
issue, however, it should conclude that the inquiry
centers on 1868.
An originalist analysis in a case challenging a
state law must focus on 1868 because “[c]onstitutional
rights are enshrined with the scope they were understood to have when the people adopted them.” See Heller, 554 U.S. at 634-35 (emphasis added). A state “is
bound to respect the right to keep and bear arms because of the Fourteenth Amendment, not the Second.”
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 37; see also id. at 71 (concluding
paragraph, stating that “New York's proper-cause requirement violates the Fourteenth Amendment”). Accordingly, in a First Amendment case, Justice Thomas
explained that he “would begin the assessment of the
scope of free-speech rights incorporated against the
States by looking to what ordinary citizens at the time
of the Fourteenth Amendment’s ratification would
have understood the right to encompass.” Mahanoy
Area Sch. Dist. v. B. L., 594 U.S. 180, 212 (2021)
(Thomas, J., dissenting) (citation omitted). Similarly,
Justice Scalia called for “further evidence of common
practice in 1868,” saying “I doubt that the Fourteenth
Amendment time-warped the post-Civil War States

29

Consideration of the full historical record, including post-ratification evidence, establishes that the
challenged assault weapon laws sit at the intersection
of multiple regulatory traditions. This includes the
tradition of restricting armed groups. That tradition
evolved in its particulars in response to changing technologies and social conditions, but remained unchanged at the level of principle: legislatures can protect their communities from mass violence by targeting the specific way in which that violence is commonly inflicted. States and local governments should
be permitted to continue that historical tradition by
keeping weapons of war out of our communities.
